summary.text: Feudalism was a mix of customs and systems that flourished in medieval Europe from the 9th to 15th centuries, built around land held in exchange for service or labour.
In its classic definition it was a set of reciprocal legal and military obligations of the warrior nobility, centred on lords, vassals, and fiefs.
A broader definition also covers the clergy and the peasantry, who were bound by a system of manorialism, so that all three estates of the realm are included.

facts.label: Where it began
facts.value: Usually where an empire decentralised, such as the Carolingian Empire

facts.label: Word in use
facts.value: The adjective feudal was in use by at least 1406

items.prompt: A historian is asked to sum up the basic bargain of the feudal system in one line. Which line fits?

options.label: Buying land from a ruler with a yearly payment of coins
Holding land in exchange for service or labour
Receiving wages from a central treasury for fighting
Choosing which employer to work for each season

items.explain: Feudalism was a way of structuring society around relationships that came from holding land in exchange for service or labour.

items.prompt: One historian limits feudalism to the warrior nobility, while another includes priests and farm workers too. What separates the two definitions?

options.label: The broader one counts all three estates, not only the nobility
The narrow one covers only the clergy and the peasantry
The broader one leaves out lords and vassals entirely
The narrow one was published before the broader one

items.explain: Ganshof's classic definition covers the obligations of the warrior nobility, while Bloch's broader one adds the clergy and the peasantry.

items.prompt: A tour guide claims that peasants in the Middle Ages proudly described their society as a formal political system called feudalism. Why is that doubtful?

options.label: Peasants were forbidden by law from naming their lords
The system only began after the 15th century had ended
Medieval people did not think of it as a formal political system
Only the clergy were ever allowed to name the system aloud

items.explain: Although the term comes from a medieval word for fief, the people of the Middle Ages did not conceive of the system as a formal political system.

items.prompt: Some medieval historians keep arguing over whether the word feudalism really helps explain medieval society. How would you describe that argument?

options.label: Ongoing, with no conclusion reached
Settled long ago, and everyone accepts the word
Settled long ago, and everyone rejects the word
Ended once the noun came into use in the 18th century

items.explain: Discussion among medieval historians over whether feudalism is a useful construct has been ongoing and inconclusive.

items.prompt: A ruler has cavalry to support but no bureaucracy to pay for it. If this follows the Carolingian pattern, what does the ruler end up doing?

options.label: Sending the horsemen home to rely on infantry
Hiring foreign soldiers with imported goods
Taxing peasants to fill a standing treasury
Giving land to the mounted soldiers

items.explain: The Carolingian Empire lacked the bureaucratic infrastructure to support cavalry without allocating land to its mounted troops.

items.prompt: Mounted soldiers in a breaking-up empire begin to pass down the land they were given. What does this do to the empire's central power?

options.label: Their power stays limited to war and never reaches daily life
Their power spreads into many areas and weakens central rule
Their power is taken back by the ruler in each generation
Their power fades quickly because heirs cannot hold the land

items.explain: Mounted soldiers secured hereditary rule over their land, and their power came to cover social, political, judicial and economic matters, which significantly diminished unitary power.
